386.title: Everyone talks of bliss
386.hook: everyone speaks of bliss, but bliss is known through the Guru (Anand 6)
386.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this sixth pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem; its opening line is often quoted in Sikh teaching about the difference between pleasure and true bliss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri four, and your line, my support. Did you catch being satisfied by a little? Today, a pauri that asks what joy really is. Day three hundred eighty-six.

Search the word happiness in any bookstore and you'll get a wall. Ten steps to joy. The happiness project. How to be happy in thirty days. Apps that track your mood. Podcasts promising bliss by Friday. Everybody's selling it. Everybody's talking about it. And somehow the people talking about it most aren't always the people who seem to have it. The sixth pauri of Anand Sahib noticed the same thing, long before the first self-help shelf. It opens with an observation that could have been written this morning. Today: everyone talks of bliss.
screen: `A WALL OF HAPPINESS BOOKS.` → `EVERYONE'S SELLING JOY.` → `FEW SEEM TO HAVE IT.`

segments.voice: The line, transliterated: anand anand sabh ko kahai, anand guroo te jaaniaa. Everyone speaks of bliss, bliss; but bliss is known through the Guru. Then, in paraphrase: true bliss is always known through the Guru, when the Beloved shows grace. By grace, wrongdoings are cut away, and the ointment of spiritual wisdom is put on the eyes. Those whose attachment has broken from within are made beautiful by the true Word. Says Nanak, this is bliss: bliss is known through the Guru. The image in the middle is worth stopping on. Giaan anjan, the ointment of wisdom. Anjan is the dark ointment people lined their eyes with. So the pauri pictures wisdom not as more information, but as something applied to your eyes, so you see differently. The world doesn't change. Your sight does. Then the key phrase: those whose attachment, moh, has broken from within. That's where the difference lies between the talk and the real thing. Much of the bliss on that bookstore wall is a new thing to grab: a purchase, a trip, a win. The pauri's bliss starts with letting go of the grabbing. It's known, the pauri says, through the Guru, as something received by grace and recognized from inside, not bought or argued into. And notice the word jaaniaa, known. Not felt for an afternoon. Known, the way you know your own front door. Sikhs don't say ordinary happiness is bad. A good meal, a good laugh, are gifts. The pauri just says there's a deeper joy, known through the Guru. Some readers put it simply: it doesn't leave when the afternoon does.
screen: `EVERYONE SPEAKS OF BLISS.` · `KNOWN THROUGH THE GURU.` · `GIAAN ANJAN: WISDOM ON THE EYES.` · `WHEN ATTACHMENT BREAKS WITHIN.` · then, large: `REAL JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what real joy felt like. Sit and breathe slowly. Think back to a moment of real joy in your life. Not excitement, not a win, but the quieter kind, the kind that stayed. Maybe holding a newborn, a moment in prayer, a long talk with someone you love, a sunrise you didn't expect. Let it come back. Notice where you feel it in your body. Notice what you weren't grabbing for at that moment. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you hold it. If you don't, just let yourself remember what real joy was like. The bell holds the time.
Everyone talks of bliss. Anand anand sabh ko kahai: everyone speaks of bliss, but bliss is known through the Guru, when attachment breaks within.
Your line: real joy. Today, when something makes you happy, ask quietly: is this the grabbing kind, or the kind that stays? Day three hundred eighty-six.

387.title: The one you bless
387.hook: only the one You bless receives this gift (Anand, early pauris)
387.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this line within the third pauri of the short Anand Sahib at the close of services; grace, nadar, is a central theme of Sikh scripture alongside honest work, service and remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri six, and your line, real joy. Did you catch the kind that stays? Today we go back to a line from pauri three that we saved. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

An arcade claw machine. A glass box full of stuffed toys, a metal claw on a joystick. You drop in your coins, steer the claw, line it up perfectly, press the button. It closes, lifts, and the toy slips out of its grip, every single time. Then there's the other way to get a toy. Someone who loves you reaches into a bag and simply hands you one. No skill involved. No coins. You just hold out your hand. A lot of life can feel like the claw machine. Anand Sahib describes the other way. Today: the one you bless.
screen: `A CLAW MACHINE: GRAB, SLIP, AGAIN.` → `OR SOMEONE SIMPLY HANDS IT TO YOU.` → `A LOT OF LIFE FEELS LIKE THE CLAW.`

segments.voice: Back in pauri three, after asking what isn't in the Master's house, the next line says, transliterated: ghar ta terai sabh kichh hai, jis deh su paavae. Everything is in your house; the one you give it to, receives. Jis deh su paavae. The one you give to, gets. That's the claw machine turned upside down. The house is full, but nobody breaks in. It's given. This runs straight through Sikh teaching. Guru Nanak puts it in the Japji, in paraphrase: by our actions we get this body, this garment, but by grace the door of liberation opens. The word there is nadar, the glance of grace, the Master's look of favor. You'll find it all over the Guru Granth Sahib. Anand Sahib keeps returning to it too: bliss is known when the Beloved shows grace. Now, a fair question. Does this mean effort doesn't matter? Sikhs would say firmly no. The same Gurus taught kirat karni, honest work, and seva, service, and daily simran. A Sikh is expected to do the work. But the work isn't a coin in a slot that buys God. It's more like holding your hands out, ready. The gift still comes as a gift. That changes how it feels to receive it. If you grabbed it, you'll grip it tight, afraid of losing it, a little proud you won. If it was given, you can hold it open-handed, grateful, and share it. You met that posture on day three hundred sixty-two, with karah prasad in cupped hands. Same idea, now in Anand. Given, not grabbed.
screen: `JIS DEH SU PAAVAE.` · `NADAR: THE GLANCE OF GRACE.` · `EFFORT STILL MATTERS.` · `HELD OPEN-HANDED, NOT GRIPPED.` · then, large: `GIVEN, NOT GRABBED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank grace for one thing. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of one good thing in your life that you know, honestly, you didn't earn. Maybe it's the family you were born into, a teacher who saw something in you, your health, a chance encounter that changed things. Hold it in your mind. Notice how differently it sits once you admit it was given. If you pray, you can thank the Giver, simply, with Waheguru. If you don't, just let yourself feel thankful, with nobody in particular to thank. The bell holds the time.
The one you bless. Jis deh su paavae: the Master's house holds everything, and the one it's given to receives it, by grace, not by grabbing.
Your line: given, not grabbed. Today, receive one thing, a compliment, a favor, a meal, without explaining why you deserve it. Just say thank you. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

388.title: Cleverness never found it
388.hook: the restless, clever mind has never found Him (Anand)
388.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem; its opening line is often quoted in Sikh teaching against cleverness and pride in spiritual life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one you bless, and your line, given, not grabbed. Did you manage to just say thank you? Today, the opposite of receiving: being clever. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

We admire clever people. The kid who finds the loophole in the rules. The friend who always knows the shortcut. The person who can argue any side and win. A lot of modern life rewards it: hack your sleep, hack your diet, hack your productivity. There's a life hack for everything. So it's a little startling when a pauri of Anand Sahib looks straight at cleverness and says, flatly, that it has never once found the One. Not rarely. Never. Nobody. Today: cleverness never found it.
screen: `WE ADMIRE THE CLEVER ONES.` → `THERE'S A HACK FOR EVERYTHING.` → `NEVER ONCE, FOR THIS.`

segments.voice: The pauri opens, transliterated: ae man chanchal chaturaaee kinai na paaiaa. O restless mind, no one has found him through cleverness. Chanchal means restless, flickering, never still, like a flame in the wind. Chaturaaee is cleverness, cunning, being smart. Kinai na paaiaa: no one has found. Then, in paraphrase: through cleverness no one has found him; listen, my mind. This enticing illusion, maya, has led people astray in doubt. And the One who made that enticing illusion is the One who set it in the world. It's the mind again, addressed directly, the way pauri two did. But this time the Guru names the mind's favorite trick. Cleverness. Why would that fail? Because cleverness is a way of getting, and you met yesterday what this tradition says about getting. Cleverness finds angles, works systems, beats the claw machine. But the One isn't a system. You can't outsmart the One who made the game. Guru Nanak says it in the Japji's first pauri too, in paraphrase: you could have a hundred thousand clevernesses, and not one goes with you. So the Gurus aren't against intelligence. The Guru Granth Sahib is full of brilliant poetry and sharp thinking. They're against using cleverness as a way around surrender. The restless mind keeps thinking there must be a trick. Anand says there isn't. The way in, Anand keeps saying, is love, and grace, and staying. No trick is needed, and none would work.
screen: `CHANCHAL: RESTLESS, LIKE A FLAME.` · `CHATURAAEE: CLEVERNESS.` · `YOU CAN'T OUTSMART THE GAME'S MAKER.` · `NOT AGAINST THINKING; AGAINST TRICKS.` · then, large: `NOT BY CLEVERNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one clever plan. Sit and breathe slowly. Notice a plan you've been working on that's a bit too clever. A way to get someone to do what you want without asking. A shortcut around something you should just face. A strategy for looking good. Hold it up to the light. Then, for today, set it down. Do the plain thing instead, ask directly, face it, be seen as you are. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let the plan go. If you don't, just notice how much lighter the plain way feels. The bell holds the time.
Cleverness never found it. Ae man chanchal chaturaaee kinai na paaiaa: O restless mind, no one has ever found the Lord through cleverness.
Your line: not by cleverness. Today, when you catch yourself working an angle, stop and choose the plain, honest way instead. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

389.title: The Word clears doubt
389.hook: the Guru's Word cuts through doubt like light through dark (Anand)
389.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and many keep kirtan or recited gurbani playing at home, especially at anxious times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cleverness, and your line, not by cleverness. Did you choose a plain way over an angle? Today, the thing that cleverness can never quite shake off: doubt. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

It's two in the morning and you're awake, and a doubt has moved in. Did I make the right choice? Do they actually like me? Is any of this real? You try to argue it away. You list the reasons. You check your phone for reassurance. You promise yourself you'll sort it out tomorrow. None of it works, because doubt doesn't leave when it loses an argument. It just waits for the next quiet moment. One pauri of Anand Sahib is about exactly this, and it says something surprising about what does and doesn't clear it. Today: the Word clears doubt.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, A DOUBT MOVES IN.` → `ARGUING IT AWAY DOESN'T WORK.` → `IT WAITS FOR THE NEXT QUIET.`

segments.voice: The word for doubt here is sahsaa, an anxious, uncertain, divided state of mind. And the pauri starts by ruling things out. In paraphrase: through rituals, sahaj, that settled ease, does not arise, and without sahaj, doubt does not go. Doubt doesn't leave however many disciplines you keep or deeds you perform. The soul is stained by doubt; what discipline could wash it clean? Then the answer: wash the mind by attaching it to the Word, the shabad, and keep your awareness on the Lord. Says Nanak, by the Guru's grace sahaj wells up, and this doubt departs. Notice the chain. Doubt goes when sahaj comes. Sahaj comes not through rituals, but through the Word and the Guru's grace. And the picture is washing. Doubt is like a stain, and the Word is like clean water. The index adds a second picture: a light in a dark room. Nobody argues with the dark, or pushes it out piece by piece. The light goes on, and the dark is simply gone. That is how the pauri treats the shabad. Not as a better argument against doubt, but as something that changes the room. It's one reason some Sikhs keep kirtan playing at home, or recite gurbani when the mind is unsettled. Not to win a debate with the doubt. It's to let the Word fill the space the doubt was living in. One honest note. The pauri isn't saying you'll never have a question. Sikhs ask hard questions; the Gurus asked them too. Sahsaa is the anxious, gnawing kind of doubt, the kind that stains. The Word, the pauri says, washes that.
screen: `SAHSAA: ANXIOUS, DIVIDED DOUBT.` · `NOT CLEARED BY RITUALS.` · `WASH THE MIND WITH THE WORD.` · `LIKE A LIGHT, NOT AN ARGUMENT.` · then, large: `THE WORD CLEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down one doubt, then rest. Grab a scrap of paper or your phone's notes. Write down one doubt that's been gnawing at you, in a single short sentence. Don't solve it. Don't argue with it. Just put it outside your head, where you can see it. Then put the paper down, or turn the screen over. Sit, and breathe slowly. If you pray, you can let Waheguru fill the space where the doubt was, or play a shabad you love. If you don't, just rest in the quiet after the doubt has been written down. The bell holds the time.
The Word clears doubt. Sahsaa, the anxious doubt that stains the mind, isn't cleared by rituals; it goes when the Word washes the mind and sahaj wells up.
Your line: the word clears. Today, when a doubt starts to gnaw, don't argue with it; put on a shabad or a quiet song and let it fill the room instead. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

390.title: Sharper than a sword
390.hook: the devotees' way is unique, sharper than a sword and finer than a hair (Anand 14)
390.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and the khanda, the double-edged sword it names, is used to stir the amrit at the Khalsa initiation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, doubt, and your line, the word clears. Did a shabad or a song fill the room? Today, pauri fourteen, and a path that's very narrow indeed. Day three hundred ninety.

Watch a child walk along a curb like a balance beam. Arms out, one foot in front of the other, eyes fixed ahead, while everyone else just walks on the sidewalk. One wobble and she's off. It takes total attention, and it's strangely absorbing. Now imagine the curb gets thinner, sharp as a blade, fine as a single hair. And imagine somebody telling you that this, not the wide sidewalk, is the path of those who love God. That's the fourteenth pauri of Anand Sahib. Today: sharper than a sword.
screen: `WALKING A CURB, ARMS OUT.` → `ONE WOBBLE AND YOU'RE OFF.` → `NOW, THINNER THAN A HAIR.`

segments.voice: The pauri opens: bhagtaa kee chaal niraalee. The way of the devotees is unique, unlike any other. Niraalee means distinct, set apart, one of a kind. Then, in paraphrase: the way of the devotees is distinct; they walk a hard path. They give up greed, grasping, ego and craving, and they don't talk too much. Then the famous image, transliterated: khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee, et maarag jaanaa. Sharper than a double-edged sword, finer than a hair: that is the path they walk. Those who, by the Guru's grace, let go of self, their desire merges into the Lord. Says Nanak, the way of the devotees, age after age, is unique. Two details stand out. First, khanniahu, from khanda, the double-edged sword. Guru Amar Das was reaching for an everyday picture of sharpness. More than a century later, in 1699, a khanda would stir the amrit at the first Khalsa initiation, and today it stands at the center of the Sikh emblem, so Sikhs now hear this line with that blade in mind. Second, look at the list of what's given up. Greed, grasping, ego, craving. And then, almost funny in its plainness: talking too much. Not some great austerity. Just fewer words. That's the hard path. It isn't hard because it's exotic. It's hard because it's narrow. Every day, a hundred small chances to step off: a greedy thought, a proud word, one more thing to grab. The devotee's way is to stay on the line, again and again. And notice how the pauri ends: the ones who stay on the line are those who, by the Guru's grace, have let go of self, and whose desire merges into the Lord.
screen: `NIRAALEE: SET APART, UNIQUE.` · `GIVE UP GREED, EGO, CRAVING.` · `AND DON'T TALK TOO MUCH.` · `SHARPER THAN A KHANDA, FINER THAN A HAIR.` · then, large: `THE NARROW WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk one narrow line carefully. If you can, stand up and find a line on the floor: a floorboard seam, the edge of a rug, a tile joint. Walk slowly along it, heel to toe, arms out if you need them, for a few steps. Notice the attention it takes. Notice how the mind goes quiet when it has one thing to do. Then sit and breathe. If you can't stand, trace a line slowly with one finger. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each careful step. The bell holds the time.
Sharper than a sword. Khanniahu tikhee vaalahu nikee: the devotees' way is sharper than a double-edged sword and finer than a hair, and walked by letting go of self.
Your line: the narrow way. Today, take the narrow way in one small thing: say fewer words in one conversation than you normally would. Day three hundred ninety.

391.title: Treasure in the Name
391.hook: the Name is a treasure found within, not in markets (Anand)
391.howItsDone: Many Sikhs understand the Name as a treasure found within through simran, the Guru's Word and the sangat, a theme that runs through Anand Sahib and the whole Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the devotees' path, and your line, the narrow way. Did you manage fewer words in one conversation? Today, the thing those devotees find on the way. Day three hundred ninety-one.

An old Indian story tells of a musk deer. A sweet, wonderful scent follows it everywhere, and it drives the deer wild. It runs through forests, over hills, nose to every flower and bush, desperate to find where the smell is coming from. It never does. Because the scent is coming from the deer itself. The musk is in its own body. It has been carrying the treasure the whole time it's been searching. Sikh teachers tell it too, and it fits Anand Sahib's theme for today. Today: treasure in the Name.
screen: `A MUSK DEER CHASING A SCENT.` → `OVER HILLS, THROUGH FORESTS.` → `THE SCENT WAS ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Anand Sahib, like much of gurbani, speaks of the Name as a treasure, one that can't be found in markets or bought with money, and, as you heard on day three hundred eighty-eight, can't be won by cleverness either. It's found within, through the Guru. That idea runs right through the Guru Granth Sahib. The Bhagat Pipa, one of the saints whose words sit in the Granth beside the Gurus, put it in one line. In paraphrase: whatever is in the universe is also in the body, and whoever searches, finds it. So the treasure isn't hidden somewhere far away. It's hidden close. Which is precisely why it's hard to find. We look outward by habit. Markets, achievements, other people's approval, the next place, the next thing. Like the deer, we're nose-down in every bush but our own. Now, a careful note. Sikh teaching doesn't call the outer world worthless. It honors the householder: honest work, family, a life lived among people. Work and markets aren't the enemy. The point is about where the treasure is kept. You can work at the market all day. You just won't find the Name for sale there. And how do you look within? The Sikh answer is simple and steady: simran, remembering the Name; the shabad, the Guru's Word; and the company of others on the same path, the sangat. These are like a lamp turned inward. Today Anand's picture for the Name is treasure. Like the deer's musk, it was carried along the whole time the searching went on.
screen: `A TREASURE NOT FOR SALE.` · `WHAT'S IN THE UNIVERSE IS IN THE BODY.` · `WORK AND MARKETS AREN'T THE ENEMY.` · `SIMRAN, SHABAD, SANGAT: A LAMP INWARD.` · then, large: `TREASURE WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look inward for one minute. Close your eyes, or lower them. Breathe slowly. Instead of following your thoughts outward, to the day's plans and people, turn your attention around, gently, toward the place the attention is coming from. Notice the breath. Notice the stillness under the thoughts. Don't try to find anything. Just look in, the way you'd look into a quiet room. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly and let it lead you in. If you don't, just rest in the looking. The bell holds the time.
Treasure in the Name. Anand's picture of the Name as a treasure found within, through the Guru, not bought in any market, like the musk deer's own scent.
Your line: treasure within. Today, when you catch yourself searching outside for something to make you feel complete, stop for one breath and look in first. Day three hundred ninety-one.

Sikh teaching honors honest work and family life. the Name just isn't for sale in the market.

a saint whose line says what's in the universe is in the body, and the searcher finds it.
the treasure, in this picture, is hidden somewhere far away
it's hidden close, within, which is why it's easy to miss.

fork.setup: you're the musk deer, running from hill to hill after a wonderful scent you can never find. what's the answer the story gives?
options: keep searching the next hill.
the scent is your own: the treasure is within.
give up on the scent entirely.
fork.reveal: the musk was in the deer's own body the whole time. Sikh teachers use the story for the Name: a treasure found within, through the Guru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nidhaan, treasure; gurbani often calls the Name a treasure found within.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about spiritual riches somewhere above.
what it means: the Name is a treasure already within, found through the Guru, simran and the sangat, not bought or won.
what a scholar hears: Bhagat Pipa's line 'jo brahmande soee pinde', what is in the cosmos is in the body, at Ang 695, gives the Granth's classic statement of the treasure within.

sources.ref: Anand Sahib, Ang 917–922 (the Name as treasure within)
Bhagat Pipa, Raag Dhanasari, Ang 695 ('jo brahmande soee pinde, jo khojai so paavai')

392.title: The unripe word
392.hook: without the True Guru, other words are unripe (Anand 24)
392.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the full Anand Sahib in the morning, and pauri 24's warning about unripe words is often cited to explain why kirtan in the gurdwara is drawn from gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, treasure in the Name, and your line, treasure within. Did you look inward for a minute and find anything there? Today, a pauri about which words are worth keeping. Day three hundred ninety-two.

A fruit stall in Amritsar. A woman picks up a mango, presses it with her thumb, and puts it back. Kacha, she says. Unripe. She tries another that gives a little and smells sweet. Pakka. Ripe. Those two words run all through Punjabi and Hindi. A kacha road is dirt; a pakka road is paved. A kacha house is mud; a pakka house is brick. Kacha means not ready yet: not fired, not finished. Guru Amar Das took that market word and set it into the Anand. Today: the unripe word.
screen: `A MANGO AT A FRUIT STALL.` → `KACHA: UNRIPE. PAKKA: RIPE.` → `A MARKET WORD IN THE ANAND.`

segments.voice: Pauri twenty-three of the Anand calls out to the Sikhs of the True Guru: come and sing the true bani, the true word. Pauri twenty-four turns the coin over. Its refrain says, in paraphrase, that without the True Guru every other word is kachee, unripe. Then the circle widens. The ones who say such words are unripe. The ones who hear them are unripe. The ones who explain them are unripe. Even someone who repeats the Lord's name all day with the tongue, the pauri says, may not understand a thing, if the mind has been carried off by maya, the pull of the passing world. So the problem isn't vocabulary. Holy words can be said in an unripe way. The pauri points at two things: where a word comes from, and the mind that receives it. For Sikhs, the ripe word is gurbani, the Gurus' own words, now gathered in the Guru Granth Sahib. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks that the kirtan sung in the congregation be gurbani, along with the writings of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. There's an everyday edge here too. Plenty of what gets said in a day is a little kacha: the half-heard rumor, the quick hot take, the reply typed before the message was finished. The pauri doesn't ask anyone to go silent. It asks whether a word has a true source, and whether it's ready.
screen: `KACHA: UNRIPE, UNFIRED, NOT READY.` · `PAURI 24: WITHOUT THE GURU, WORDS ARE RAW.` · `SPEAKER, HEARER, EXPLAINER: ALL UNRIPE.` · `RIPE: A TRUE SOURCE, A PRESENT MIND.` · then, large: `RIPE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think back over the last day of talking. Let one sentence come up that was a little kacha: said too fast, said half true, said to win. Don't argue with it. Just notice it, the way the woman at the stall feels the mango and sets it down. Then rest with the breath. Let the next thing you say aloud today get one full breath to ripen first. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, quietly, and let the rest be silence. The bell holds the time.

The unripe word. Kachee baanee: in the Anand, any word that doesn't come from the True Guru, or is said by a mind somewhere else. This week: bliss known through the Guru, given not grabbed, the narrow way, treasure within, and now ripe words.
Your line: ripe words. Today, before you send a message or answer a hard question, take one breath and ask whether it's ready. If it isn't, let it wait. Day three hundred ninety-two.

match.prompt: ripe and unripe — tap the pairs.
pairs: without the True Guru, words are unripe

myth: pauri 24 says only the speakers of unripe words are unripe
it names the speakers, the hearers and the explainers too.
the pauri says holy words can still be said in an unripe way
a tongue can repeat the Name while the mind is carried off by maya.
the Rehat Maryada asks that congregational kirtan come from gurbani and a few named writers
gurbani, with the writings of Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal.

fork.setup: a message makes you angry and your reply is already typed. by the logic of pauri 24, what would make it ripe?
options: using the right holy words in it.
its source, and a mind that is actually present.
sending it fast, before the moment passes.
fork.reveal: the pauri says even the Lord's name can be said unripely; ripeness depends on where a word comes from and the mind behind it.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kachee, unripe or raw; pauri 24's refrain calls every word without the True Guru kachee.

trapdoor: what you thought: an unripe word is just a rude or harsh one.
what it means: a word that doesn't come from the Guru, or is said by a mind elsewhere; even holy words can be unripe.
what a scholar hears: kacha and pakka are the everyday Punjabi pair for raw and ripe, unfired and fired; Guru Amar Das builds the refrain of pauri 24 on that market word.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on kirtan in the congregation
